## `src/transport/backend.rs`

### src/transport/backend.rs:98

````text
Faithful to `SSHClient::from_env`, which applies this flag but
`SSHRunner::from_config` does not.
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:109

````text
The capacity invariant is checked here rather than in
`Config::from_env` because only the native backend has a
per-endpoint session ceiling — see `scheduler::validate_capacity`.
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:114

````text
Native backend requires a running transport daemon reachable via
IPC. The daemon holds the connection pool and multiplexes requests;
connecting directly would bypass the pool and re-open SSH per op.
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:132

````text
Native on non-Unix (Windows) is not yet supported — the IPC transport
is Unix-domain-socket only. Report UnsupportedBackend rather than
silently falling back to a direct connection (which would bypass the
daemon/pool design).
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:138

````text
Without the feature, `native` is not compiled in — report the
structured error instead of silently using OpenSSH.
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:203

````text
Minimal Config for these tests — only backend selection matters here.
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:258

````text

builds without the feature.
````

````text
`Arc<dyn RemoteTransport>` is not `Debug`, so neither `unwrap_err`
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:283


````text
OpenSSH multiplexes over ControlMaster and has no per-endpoint
````

### src/transport/backend.rs:321

## `src/transport/contract.rs`

### src/transport/contract.rs:669

````text
An expired deadline fails before any remote work is attempted, and the
failure is classified as QueueTimeout — which is what makes it safe
to retry.
````

### src/transport/contract.rs:680

````text
Forwarding is not yet provided by any shipping backend; the contract
requires it to be reported, not panicked on.
````

### src/transport/contract.rs:724

````text
Deadline must outlast the execution timeout by the startup
allowance, so a request is never doomed by its own timeout.
````

### src/transport/contract.rs:782

````text
Two OutcomeUnknown errors with contradictory messages must classify
identically — that is what "no message-string matching" means.
````

### src/transport/contract.rs:862

````text
Configuration-ish failures stay usage errors; everything else stays a
general error, matching VirtuosoError's existing classification.
````

## `src/transport/identity.rs`

### src/transport/identity.rs:148

````text
`comm` is parenthesised and may contain spaces and parens, so split
on the *last* ')' and index from there.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:152

````text
Field 3 is `state`, so field 22 (`starttime`) is index 19.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:192

````text
Return the raw errno so callers can distinguish "no such
process" from a genuine read failure. Matching on the formatted
`io::Error` text would never match: it renders as
"No such process (os error 3)", not "ESRCH".
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:219

````text
On macOS an absent PID is *not* an error: sysctl succeeds with a
zero-length result (errno ESRCH is not reported). Verified against
pids 41000 / 99999 / 999999, which return ret=0 len=0.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:237

````text
KERN_PROCARGS2 is a top-level KERN_* entry, not a KERN_PROC
subcommand: three elements, not four.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:243

````text
Same zero-length convention as `start_time`.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:267

````text
Both attributes are mandatory: a partially-read identity must fail
closed rather than compare as "empty equals empty".
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:329

````text
All fallible Win32 calls are written out sequentially rather than
inside a closure: an `unsafe` block does not extend into a closure
body, and this module cannot be compiled off-Windows to catch that.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:336

````text
A pid that is not in use fails this way; anything else
(access denied on a protected process) is a read failure.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:380

````text
`size` is the written length in u16 code units.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:440

````text
Same PID, different process: the whole reason PID alone is rejected.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:476

````text
The property that closes the Windows `taskkill /F` gap: where the
identity cannot be read, the answer is a refusal.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:498

````text
The same PID looked up again yields the same identity.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:515

````text
Always true: the parsed start time must be in the past and, for a
test process, within the last day. This alone catches an
endianness or offset mistake in the kinfo_proc read.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:529

````text
Cross-check against `ps`, which reads the same value through
libproc. Sandboxed runners may forbid spawning it, in which case the
plausibility checks above are the assertion.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:545

````text
ps prints e.g. "Sun Aug 30 05:20:00 2026" — the trailing year.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:562

````text
`KERN_PROCARGS2` may report the path the process was invoked with, so
compare the resolved file name rather than the full path.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:585

````text
Distinct processes must produce distinct markers.
````

### src/transport/identity.rs:592

````text
Regression guard: errno must be mapped by *code* (ESRCH), not by
matching the formatted `io::Error` text, which reads
"No such process (os error 3)" and never contains "ESRCH".
Not `u32::MAX`: as a `c_int` that is -1, which the kernel handles
specially rather than reporting ESRCH. macOS pid_max is 100000.
````

## `src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs`

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:25

````text
The wire payload types live in `ipc::server`, which is gated on
`(unix, any(test, feature = "native-ssh"))`. Mirror that gate here so the
import disappears in builds where the server is absent.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:63

````text
Set a generous default socket timeout (5 minutes). Individual
`exchange()` calls tighten this to the request's remaining deadline
before reading the response, so long-running commands (large file
transfers, slow SKILL evals) are not cut off at 5 seconds.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:89

````text
Tier-1 is a one-shot probe, not a long-running operation. A short
deadline keeps `tunnel stop` responsive even when the daemon has
hung the socket open without serving.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:143

````text
Acquire the shared connection mutex with a deadline. A long-running
request holding the lock must not cause a short-deadline request to
wait indefinitely — try_lock polls and bails when the deadline passes.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:147

````text
Re-check after acquiring the lock: the deadline may have passed
while we were waiting. Don't send a request whose budget is gone.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:157

````text
Write under the absolute deadline: every partial write re-applies
the remaining budget as the socket send timeout, so back-pressure
cannot accumulate beyond the total deadline.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:165

````text
Read the full frame under the same absolute deadline — every
partial read re-applies the remaining budget, so a multi-segment
response cannot reset the timer on every underlying read().
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:235

````text
Handshake should complete in well under a second on a healthy daemon.
Use a 5s absolute deadline with dynamic socket timeouts.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:463

````text
The real `server` module is the source of truth — this test exists
only to verify the client (NativeTransportClient) still round-trips
through a server that uses it.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:472

````text
The bound the design calls a hard requirement.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:486

````text
The step-0 shared suite must pass over the IPC path exactly as it does
for the OpenSSH backend.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:490

````text
Extra: a successful command and a transfer round-trip through the daemon.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:520

````text
Give the thread time to acquire the lock.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:522

````text
Try to acquire with a 500ms deadline — must fail in <2s.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:587

````text
Thread A: long request (will hold the mutex for ~2s on server side).
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:592

````text
Give thread A time to acquire the mutex and send its request.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:595

````text
Thread B: short deadline — must time out in ~1s, not wait for A's 2s.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:621

````text
Server: handshake, then for every request write the frame prefix and
1 byte of payload every 500ms — a 4-byte response takes ~2s, which
exceeds the 1s deadline.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:667

````text
1s deadline — the slow 2s response must be cut off at ~1s.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:716

````text
For each request: wait 0.9s, send frame header (100-byte payload),
then stop sending — the client must time out on the second read.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:726

````text
4-byte big-endian length = 100, then no payload.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:731

````text
Stop sending payload. Loop back to read — when the
client times out and drops the connection, read_frame
returns EOF and we exit.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:747

````text
With dynamic timeouts: 0.9s (header) + ~0.1s (second read) = ~1.0s.
Without it: 0.9s + 1.0s = ~1.9s. Allow 1.3s for scheduling jitter.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:771

````text
Channel keeps the server alive without reading the socket. The server
blocks on recv() until the test tells it to exit — it never drains the
receive buffer, so the client's send buffer fills and write() blocks.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:793

````text
Block here — do NOT read any request frames. The client's send
buffer fills and write() blocks on back-pressure.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:800

````text
Explicitly cap the client's send buffer at 8 KiB so a 1 MiB upload is
guaranteed to block in write() — no reliance on the system default.
(Linux doubles the value for bookkeeping, so actual is ~16 KiB.)
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:823

````text
1 MiB text upload — far larger than the 8 KiB send buffer, so the
write will block once the buffer fills. Use an explicit 1s deadline.
````

### src/transport/ipc/daemon.rs:841

````text
Must be close to the 1s budget — not instant (which would mean no
back-pressure and a fake pass) and not far over it.
````

## `src/transport/ipc/server.rs`

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:36

````text
Used only by `run`/`run_with_pool`, which are feature-gated; the test module
imports its own.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:41

````text
`run`/`run_with_pool` are the only consumers of these, and they are
feature-gated, so the imports must carry the same gate — ungated, a
feature-off build reports them unused.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:61

````text
`EndpointKey`/`EndpointPool`/`Priority`/`SchedulerLimits` are consumed only

feature-gated — gate the imports to match so a feature-off build does not

````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:70

````text
`ShutdownCoordinator` is consumed only by the feature-gated `run`/`run_with_pool`
and `ShutdownState::coordinator`; gate the import to match.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:251

````text
Parse the hello body just to confirm the profile is a string — we don't
gate on profile name yet (the daemon is per-profile, so this is mostly a
sanity check).
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:400

````text
A peer that doesn't even send Hello is not a client we should
answer — close silently. (An active attacker would learn nothing
here that isn't in the public protocol spec.)
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:417

````text
Dispatch loop. The connection is "active work" from the shutdown
coordinator's perspective for as long as this loop runs.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:424

````text
Phase 1 has fired: stop taking new work on this connection too.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:442

````text
Fire the token BEFORE writing the ack: once the client observes the
ack, "shutdown was accepted" is already true everywhere. The
reverse order would let a client act on the ack while the accept
loop is still serving. In-flight requests on *other* connections
keep running until the grace expires.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:460

````text
Resolve the transport for this request. A failure here is a daemon
problem (no connection can be created), reported as an error frame
— it does not tear down the accept loop.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:479

````text
A connection-level failure means the pooled transport is no longer
trustworthy. Evict it so the next request reconnects instead of
serving from a dead connection. The generation captured before
dispatch is the safety net: a fresh endpoint built by a concurrent
request stays alive even when this callback is late.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:498

````text
Peer closed — bail out of the loop. We don't try to recover
half-written state: every operation is idempotent or reports
`OutcomeUnknown`, and the next request will start fresh.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:527

````text
Meter every transport-touching operation on the endpoint scheduler.
Challenge/Shutdown/Hello never touch the wire, so they must not
consume a session.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:548

````text
Capture the generation of the endpoint we are about to serve on.
The eviction callback uses it to drop the connection only when the
slot still holds the same instance — a fresh replacement built
concurrently must survive a late callback from a request that
already failed.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:677

````text
Tier-1 liveness proof: the daemon echoes its nonce. The parent
CLI compares the answer to its recorded `daemon_nonce` to prove
the process on the other end of the socket is the recorded
daemon instance. We deliberately do not include the auth_token
in the answer — anyone who could present the token has already
passed the handshake; this operation is the *separate* check
that runs before auth is granted.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:726

````text
Mode 0600: only the current user can connect. The owner is set by the
bind above; chmod enforces the bits regardless of umask.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:737

````text
Non-blocking accept + poll: the token is fired from a worker thread (a
connection that sent `Shutdown`), and a blocking accept would never see
it until the next connection arrived.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:773

````text
Restore blocking mode on the accepted stream: on macOS an
accepted socket inherits O_NONBLOCK from the listener, and
a non-blocking stream would make every frame read return
`WouldBlock` immediately.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:784

````text
A spurious accept error is not fatal: the listener is still
alive and the next connection might succeed. We deliberately
do not return here — a transient resource exhaustion should
not tear down the daemon.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:792

````text
Three-phase shutdown: admission is already stopped (the loop broke);
wait for in-flight connections within the grace, then return — the
daemon process exits and reaps any straggler stuck in a transport call.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:858

````text
Best-effort unlink on every exit path: a stale socket from a crashed
previous run is cleaned up by `bind_listener`, but a clean exit must
also leave no artefact behind so the next daemon can rebind.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:902

````text
Best-effort unlink on every exit path — see `run` for the rationale.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:958

````text
A real round-trip beyond the suite: a command, an upload, a probe.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:981

````text
Use the raw framing layer to do a Hello with the wrong token and
inspect the server's reply.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1102

````text
Two independent IPC sessions, both resolving to the same key. The
first creates the endpoint; the second must reuse it.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1157

````text
Factory hands out a transport that fails at the connection level the
first time and works afterwards.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1186

````text
Session 1: the pooled transport fails at the connection level. The
client sees the error and the pool must evict the connection.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1223

````text
Session 2: a fresh connection is created and reports the business
failure (exit 7) — which must NOT evict it.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1271

````text
Short grace so the test does not sit through the 10 s default.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1292

````text
`run` must return Ok on its own — no process exit, no SIGKILL.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1319

````text
Keep the suffix short: macOS runners resolve `temp_dir()` to a long
`/var/folders/.../T` path and a Unix socket's `sun_path` holds at
most 104 bytes. A longer name fails to bind and the daemon never
comes up — on macOS only, which makes it easy to misread as a
platform bug in the server.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1335

````text
The key here only has to be a stable identity for the duration of
this test; no SSH is exercised. Construct it directly rather than
through `from_config` so this test module does not depend on a
full `Config`.
````

### src/transport/ipc/server.rs:1385

````text
Serve one real command first. `Hello` is answered before the
dispatch loop and `Shutdown` breaks out of it before the transport
is resolved, so without this the factory would never run and the
test would not exercise the pooled path at all.
````

## `src/transport/lifecycle.rs`

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:872

````text
Stagger the spawns so arrival order is deterministic. Without
this the assertion would be about the OS thread scheduler rather
than about our own FIFO: a waiter that happens to enqueue second
is legitimately served second.
The *recording* order needs no such care: with a single slot,
waiter `i` cannot return from `acquire` until waiter `i-1` has
dropped its permit, which happens after it recorded itself.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:891

````text
total=3, reserve=1 → two non-urgent slots, both held by normal work,
with normal waiters queued behind them. An urgent waiter must go
first once a slot frees.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:938

````text
Urgent work may overtake *queued* work only. A running request keeps
its slot until it finishes — including the reserved slot, once it is
taken: filling the total blocks even urgent work.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:952

````text
Strict priority would let a steady stream of normal commands starve
bulk transfers forever, because bulk is the lowest class and has no
reserved slot. This asserts the escape valve: once a bulk waiter has
waited past the grace it is scheduled as `Normal`.
Both non-reserved slots are held for the whole test, so the waiter
cannot be admitted either way — what is observed is the promotion
itself, not an admission.
Both phases anchor on `enqueued_at`, the timestamp the spawned thread
stamps when it acquires the mutex. The previous version used a fixed
`thread::sleep(30ms)` which raced with the OS scheduler: on slow CI
runners the test thread's lock acquisition could land >100ms past
`enqueued_at`, making Phase 1 observe `Normal` instead of `Bulk` for
a reason unrelated to the promotion logic. `enqueued_at` is captured
in the same critical section as the observed `now`, which makes the
elapsed-at-observation a *property of the data* and not of the
*moment we happened to grab the lock*.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:987

````text
Phase 1: wait for the bulk waiter to be enqueued, then verify it is
still inside the grace window. If the wait's not in the queue within
a generous deadline, panic with a clear message; if it is but the
scheduling latency already exceeds the grace, panic with the
*observable* cause instead of an opaque `left: Normal, right: Bulk`.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:996

````text
Same critical section: read both timestamps while the state
is held, so `effective_priority(now, enqueued_at)` uses a
`now` that cannot race with the waiter's continued waiting.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:1023

````text
Phase 2: sleep until we are *deterministically* past `enqueued_at +
grace`, then verify the waiter is promoted to `Normal`. The `+ 50ms`
margin absorbs the latency between waking from `sleep` and the test
thread grabbing the mutex; the anchor makes the total wall-clock
duration independent of how slow the scheduler is — only the
arithmetic `target - now` matters.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:1054

````text
Reduction is permanent and never creates a second connection.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:1062

````text

with nowhere to go.
````

### src/transport/scheduler.rs:1072

````text
2 total, 1 reserved → normal is full, urgent still has a slot.
````

````text
is pinned explicitly because `-v` only raises the level when the
````

````text
No `-f`: the spawned process IS the forward-holding ssh, so its pid

````

### src/transport/tunnel.rs:784

````text
Only THIS ssh's forward counts as success. `wait_for_forward` needs
the ssh child alive AND a reachable port AND its stderr showing it
bound the local port — a pre-existing service can never satisfy the
stderr marker, so it cannot masquerade as our tunnel. Any failure
reaps the child so the caller can try another local port without
leaking a process.
The budget covers the full SSH handshake + auth, which can be slow
through a jump host; failures (`ExitOnForwardFailure`) are detected
immediately by the child exiting, not by the budget running out.
````

````text
---- wait_for_forward -------------------------------------------------
The regression these guard against: the old success check probed only
the local TCP port, so when the port was already served by another
process (and ssh exited on bind failure) the tunnel was reported as
established. `wait_for_forward` now requires ssh's own stderr bind
marker (`Local forwarding listening on 127.0.0.1 port <n>`) — only that
proves THIS ssh bound the port; a foreign listener can never produce it.
Budgets here are deliberately short: production uses
`TUNNEL_FORWARD_BUDGET`, but every failure mode these tests exercise is
detected without waiting it out, so the whole group runs in ~3 s.
````

````text
coordinates before xdotool fires at the wrong location. On xwininfo
failure or unparseable output, fall through with default geometry

geometry is zero-sized, reject immediately without an SSH round-trip.
Coordinate bounds always use fresh xwininfo — the cache only answers
"is this window minimized?".
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2574

````text
xdotool key --window <id> <key>...
xdotool separates chord modifiers/keys with `+` (e.g. `ctrl+s`).
Older xdotool releases (e.g. 3.20200624.1) reject the hyphenated
form `ctrl-s`, and no X11 keysym name contains a hyphen, so
normalizing `-` to `+` is safe and makes `key --text "ctrl-s"`
work across xdotool versions.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2589

````text
xdotool type --window <id> -- <text>
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2592

````text
xdotool type drives XTestFakeKeyEvent and only supports ASCII
keysyms. Non-ASCII text (CJK, emoji, full-width) is silently
dropped by xdotool — detect it upfront and fail loudly instead
of reporting a false success.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2609

````text
Two-step click: first move cursor to the window-relative point,
then issue the click. `--` separator before coords protects
negative-valued x/y from being parsed as xdotool flags.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2621

````text

````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2633

````text
Step 2: xdotool click --window <id> <button>
`click [options] button` — the button is a POSITIONAL
argument; there is no `--button` option on click/mousedown/
mouseup in any xdotool release.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2644

````text
Absolute screen click: move the pointer to (x, y) in root-window
coordinates, then click on the window. Unlike click-rel, x/y are
absolute (not window-relative) screen pixels. `--` protects
negative coordinates from being parsed as xdotool flags.
````


### src/transport/x11.rs:2674

````text
True drag: mousedown -> mousemove_relative -> mouseup.
Only press/release target the window; the relative move in
between is global pointer motion and carries no window id.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2686

````text
press — button is positional, there is no `--button` option
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2696

````text
move relatively
Relative pointer motion is its OWN command: `--relative` is
not a mousemove option (it belongs to the window command
`windowmove`), and `mousemove_relative` takes no `--window`
because a delta needs no window-relative origin. `--` keeps
negative deltas from being parsed as flags.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2719

````text
xdotool mouse-button scroll: 4=up, 5=down, 6=left, 7=right.
direction + optional count come from --text ("down" or "down:3").
Optional x/y move the pointer to a window-relative point first
(defaults to the window center when omitted).
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2738

````text
repeats the whole press/release cycle, which for scroll buttons
produces a scroll tick per click.
````


### src/transport/x11.rs:2786

````text
xdotool windowminimize <id> — the window id is positional; this
subcommand accepts no options in any xdotool release. Supported

````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2795

````text
True maximization: set the WM _NET_WM_STATE MAXIMIZED_* atoms via
`xdotool windowstate --add`. This is the only X11-maximize API
xdotool exposes — `windowmaximize` is NOT a real xdotool command.
`windowstate` itself was added in xdotool 3.20210804.1, so this
operation requires a newer xdotool than the rest of the tool.
We deliberately do NOT raise the global minimum version (declared
3.20140419.1) for the whole CLI just to cover this one operation;
on older xdotool the runner returns xdotool's own error, which is
clearer than silently failing to maximize. Documented in README.
````

### src/transport/x11.rs:2817

````text
A double click is two full press/release cycles on the same
button: `xdotool click --repeat 2 --delay 60 <button>`. `--repeat`
is supported by every modern xdotool (since ~2010).
````
